DSC 106  |  Project 2: Persuasive or Deceptive Visualization

Does New York’s complaint system hold police accountable?

Dhruv Mittal (dmittal@ucsd.edu), Raunak Saluja (rsaluja@ucsd.edu), Thalesh Gupta (thgupta@ucsd.edu)

Proposition“The NYPD’s civilian complaint system rarely holds officers accountable.”

Same data, two opposite arguments. ProPublica’s dataset has 33,358 allegations against NYPD officers, each ruled substantiated, unsubstantiated, or exonerated by the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB). Switch between the two sides below.

Design decisions, scored from −2 (deceptive) to +2 (earnest). Tap one to see why we made it and what else we tried.

Grouping exonerated with unsubstantiatedTurns two outcomes into one 75.1%−1›

We used Gestalt grouping to make two outcomes read as one: unsubstantiated and exonerated share a light blue-teal family (similarity), and a bracket wraps them (enclosure), with the 75.1% label colored to match, which our checkpoint feedback suggested. Substantiated is the only dark segment, so it pops out as the small exception. The catch is that exonerated means the conduct happened and was within NYPD rules, so it isn’t really the system failing.

Alternatives. Three separate bars made readers add 46% and 29% themselves, which killed the punch. Merging them into one segment was stronger but too easy to call out, and it would hide data, so we kept both segments visible.

Counting “not substantiated” instead of substantiatedTall bars instead of short ones−1›

Chart 2 is a calculated field: the share of each category that was unsubstantiated or exonerated. It’s the same information as 13–30% substantiated, but bars at 70–87% feel like failure, and “nearly 9 in 10” sounds worse than “1 in 8.” Since bar length on a common baseline is one of the most accurately read channels, the reader takes in those big numbers instantly.

Alternatives. We first plotted the substantiation rate. The bars were short and Force just looked like a low number, not a failure. Lecture said the strongest deceptive choices come from counting differently rather than axis tricks, so this flip was where we put our effort.

Sorting by rate and making only Force pop outLeads with the worst category−0.5›

Color hue is pre-attentive, so we used it for one job: Force is dark and the other three are gray. The eye lands on Force before reading anything, and the annotation calls it “the most serious category.” Abuse of authority is the biggest category (20,292 allegations) with the best rate, but sorting puts it last and grayed out.

Alternatives. Our checkpoint used four different colors. Since the bars were already separated by position, the extra hues didn’t add information, and they split attention across all four. Alphabetical order would have put Abuse of authority first, which works against our side.

Allegations, not complaints, as the unitPicks the unit with the lowest rate−0.5›

One complaint can have several allegations, and usually only one of them gets substantiated. Counting allegations gives 24.9% substantiated, while counting complaints gives 32%. The unit is written on the chart, so it’s disclosed, but most readers won’t stop to think about it.

Alternatives. We also tried counting officers, but every officer in this dataset has at least one substantiated allegation (that’s how ProPublica built it), so that would have argued against us.

Takeaway titles with exact numbersSounds neutral, so it’s trusted+1.5›

Each title is the one thing we want readers to remember, stated with a real number (“Three in four…,” “Nearly 9 in 10…”), and every chart has a source line and a note on how the numbers were calculated. This sounds like reporting, which makes people trust it more.

Alternatives. We wrote “Most complaints against NYPD officers go nowhere” first. It’s punchier, but the rubric warns that charged language is easy to spot, so we let the numbers carry the slant instead.

Design decisions, scored from −2 (deceptive) to +2 (earnest). Tap one to see why we made it and what else we tried.

Only showing 2007–2015Starts at the low, ends at the peak−1.5›

2007 is the lowest year since 2000 and 2015 is the peak. After that the allegation rate fell to 25% in 2017, which breaks the climb. The chart gives a reason right on it: the data only has closed cases, so recent years may be incomplete. That’s true, but it’s also convenient, since it was never the real reason we cut there.

Alternatives. The full 1985–2019 range has tiny early samples and a dip after 2015. 2011–2015 looked even steeper but was so short that it seemed suspicious. Our checkpoint feedback pointed us to 2007–2015 as the version that reads as natural.

Counts with a “3x” arrowA bigger jump than the rate−0.5›

Counts went from 268 to 812, which feels more dramatic than a rate going up. Part of that is just more allegations coming in, and we say so in the subtitle (“grew only 22%”). The word “only” and the highlighted 2015 bar push readers to give the CCRB credit for all of it.

Alternatives. We tried a stacked bar of substantiated vs. not per year. It was more honest about volume, but the growth got lost in the tall stacks, so we kept counts and put the rate in the next chart.

Switching to the complaint-level rate“Half of complaints” beats “a third of allegations”−1›

The main line counts complaints with at least one substantiated allegation, which hits 50% in 2015, compared to 35% for allegations. This is the opposite unit choice from the For side. The line is directly labeled with what it counts, so it’s accurate, but the switch is easy to miss.

Alternatives. A legend would have made readers match line colors back and forth, so we used direct labels next to each line. The labels also make the bigger number feel like the main point.

Adjusting for allegation typesA real check, shown as a redundant encoding+1.5›

Someone could argue the rate only rose because the types of complaints changed, for example fewer Force allegations. So we calculated each year’s rate per category and weighted them by the 2007 mix. The dashed line still goes from 14% to 34%. It’s dashed and a different color (a redundant encoding), so it still reads in grayscale or for colorblind readers.

Alternatives. We considered leaving it out, since it makes the main line look less special. We kept it because an honest check that agrees with you is the most convincing thing you can show.

Starting the y-axis at 10%Makes the lines steeper−1›

Starting the line chart at 10% steepens both lines. People accept truncated line charts more than truncated bar charts, so it isn’t noticed. We kept the bar chart at zero because bar length is the encoding there, and a cut baseline would distort it in an obvious way.

Alternatives. We tested a dual-axis version with counts and the rate together. Lecture said relying on axis tricks caps you at satisfactory, and it looked gimmicky, so this small truncation is the only axis choice we kept.

Try it yourself: how the window changes the story

Most of our argument comes from which years we show and what we count. Move the sliders or switch the unit, and watch the headline change.

Reflection

Going in, we thought deceptive charts were mostly about stretched axes and weird scales. That turned out to be the least powerful tool we had. Every number on this page is correct, and the two sides disagree because of three quiet choices: which years to show, whether to count allegations or complaints, and what counts as “accountability.” The For side flips substantiated into “not substantiated.” The Against side switches to complaints and stops at 2015. Neither one changes a single data point. The Against side was harder to build since the overall numbers look bad for the CCRB, but once we framed it as change over time, it came together fast. Honestly, that was a little scary.

What changed our view most was finding out how framed the data already was. ProPublica only kept officers still on the force in mid-2020 with at least one substantiated allegation (we checked, and every officer in the file has one), plus only closed cases, with “unfounded” allegations dropped. So the true substantiation rate across all complaints is probably lower than anything we show, and even our earnest charts sit on someone else’s choices. We also noticed that our most honest decisions, like the category adjustment and the plain titles, made our charts more convincing, not less. Our TA suggested cutting to 2007–2015 to strengthen the Against side, and it worked so well that it made us realize how normal cherry-picking can look when there’s a reasonable-sounding note attached.

Our working definition now: a visualization is ethical if the reader would still agree with it after seeing every choice we made. The explorer above is our attempt at that test. Drag the window to 2015–2019 and the “accountability is improving” story falls apart, while switching to complaints makes almost any window look better. Choices that survive the reader finding out, like stating the unit or adjusting for category mix, feel like fair persuasion to us. Choices that only work if nobody looks, like ending at the peak year, are misleading even when they’re technically disclosed. A lot of what we did sits in the middle, which is why we don’t think there’s a clean line, just a question you have to keep asking.

Data: ProPublica, Civilian Complaints Against New York City Police Officers (CCRB data, July 2020). Static charts made in Python (pandas, matplotlib); the explorer is plain JavaScript and SVG.
